'''Richard Robson''' {{Post-nominals|country=AUS|FAA|FRS}} (born 4 June 1937) is an English and Australian chemist and Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of Melbourne]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.eoas.info/biogs/P003792b.htm | title=Robson, Richard – Biographical entry – Encyclopedia of Australian Science}}</ref> Robson specialises in [[coordination polymers]], particularly [[metal-organic framework]]s.<ref name="Hoskins-1989">{{Cite journal|title = Infinite polymeric frameworks consisting of three dimensionally linked rod-like segments|journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society|date = 1989|pages = 5962–5964|volume = 111|issue = 15|doi = 10.1021/ja00197a079|language = EN|first1 = Bernard F.|last1 = Hoskins|first2 = Richard|last2 = Robson| bibcode=1989JAChS.111.5962H }}</ref> He has been described as "a pioneer in crystal engineering involving [[transition metals]]".<ref name="Wise1998">{{cite book|first=Donald|last=Wise|title=Electrical and Optical Polymer Systems: Fundamentals: Methods, and Applications|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zHSO2GUV9ucC&pg=PA872|date=27 March 1998|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-0-8247-0118-5|page=872}}</ref><ref name="BattenNeville2009">{{cite book|author1=Stuart R. Batten|author2=Suzanne M. Neville|author3=David R. Turner|title=Coordination Polymers: Design, Analysis and Application|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iuixgwRs2eQC&pg=PA19|year=2009|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|isbn=978-0-85404-837-3|page=19}}</ref> In 2025, he was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] jointly with [[Susumu Kitagawa]] and [[Omar M. Yaghi]] for the development of metal-organic frameworks.<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 October 2025 |title=Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025 Summary |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2025/summary/ |access-date=8 October 2025 |website=[[The Nobel Prize]]}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Robson was born in [[Glusburn]], [[West Yorkshire]] (now [[North Yorkshire]]), England, on 4 June 1937.<ref name="NobelPrize.Org" /><ref name="o192">{{cite web | title=Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025 | website=[[The Nobel Prize]] | url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2025/robson/facts/ | access-date=8 October 2025}}</ref> He read chemistry at [[Brasenose College, Oxford]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bnc.ox.ac.uk/about-brasenose/news/2953-professor-richard-robson-nobel-prize-winner|title=Professor Richard Robson – Nobel Prize Winner|date=8 October 2025|website=bnc.ox.ac.uk}}</ref> earning a BA in 1959 and a DPhil in 1962.<ref name="RS">{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/richard-robson-35839/|title=Richard Robson FRS|website=Royal Society |access-date=8 October 2025}}</ref><ref name="NobelPrize.Org">{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2025/press-release/|title=Press release|website=[[The Nobel Prize]]|access-date=8 October 2025}}</ref> His doctoral research, supervised by John A. Barltrop at the [[Dyson Perrins Laboratory]], focused on the [[photochemistry]] of organic molecules.<ref>{{cite book|title=Chemistry at Oxford: A History from 1600 To 2005|first1=R. J. P.|last1=Williams|first2=John S. |last2=Rowlinson|first3=Allan|last3=Chapman|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|year=2008|isbn=978-1-84755-885-5|page=242}}</ref><ref name="i311">{{cite journal | last1=Barltrop | first1=J.A. | last2=Robson | first2=R. | title=The photochemistry of some charge-transfer complexes of cyclohexene | journal=Tetrahedron Letters | volume=4 | issue=9 | date=1963 | doi=10.1016/S0040-4039(01)90680-X | pages=597–600 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S004040390190680X | access-date=8 October 2025| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Robson conducted postdoctoral research at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (1962–64) and [[Stanford University]] (1964–65) under [[Henry Taube]] before accepting a lectureship in chemistry at the University of Melbourne in 1966, where he remained for the rest of his career.<ref name="RS"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abrahams |first=Brendan F. |last2=Batten |first2=Stuart R. |last3=D'Alessandro |first3=Deanna M. |date=2019 |title=Professor Richard Robson FAA |url=https://research.monash.edu/en/publications/professor-richard-robson-faa |journal=Australian Journal of Chemistry |language=English |volume=72 |issue=10 |pages=729 |doi=10.1071/CHv72n10_FO |issn=0004-9425 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008124427/https://research.monash.edu/en/publications/professor-richard-robson-faa |archive-date=8 October 2025 |access-date=21 November 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Research ==
Richard Robson's groundbreaking research established foundational principles in the field of coordination polymers, particularly for infinite polymeric frameworks—later termed [[metal–organic framework]]s (MOFs).<ref name="Hoskins-1989" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bruin |first=Tyler |date=24 November 2023 |title=Professor Richard Robson elected Fellow of the Royal Society |url=https://about.unimelb.edu.au/news-resources/awards-and-achievements/awards-and-prizes/professor-richard-robson-elected-fellow-of-the-royal-society |access-date=25 November 2024 |publisher=University of Melbourne |language=en}}</ref> His interest in the field was sparked in 1974 while constructing large wooden models of crystalline structures for first-year chemistry lectures.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://doi.org/10.1002/tcr.202400038|last=Robson|first=Richard|title=The Historical Development of the Concepts Underlying the Design and Construction of Targeted Coordination Polymers/MOFs: A Personal Account|journal=The Chemical Letter|volume=24|article-number=202400038|year=2024 |issue=5 |doi=10.1002/tcr.202400038 |pmid=38775251 |doi-access=free|hdl=11343/351173|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

In the 1990s, Robson created a new class of coordination polymers that underpinned an entire modern field of chemistry.<ref name="Pursuit">{{Cite web |title=The man who built a whole new field of chemistry |publisher=University of Melbourne |url=https://pursuit.unimelb.edu.au/articles/the-man-who-built-a-whole-new-field-of-chemistry |access-date=25 November 2024 |website=Pursuit |language=en}}</ref> His innovative approach used copper(I), which favours a tetrahedral geometry, in combination with a custom-designed tetranitrile organic linker.<ref name="Pursuit" /> This method produced crystalline scaffolds with a diamond-like structure but with significant, engineered void space within the framework.<ref name="Pursuit" />

== Honors and awards ==
[[File:2025 Nobel laureates in chemistry at Stockholm University.jpg|thumb|Robson with [[Susumu Kitagawa]] and [[Omar Yaghi]]]]
Robson received the Burrows Award from the Inorganic Division of The [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] in 1998 and was elected a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] in 2000.<ref name="k890">{{cite web | last=Sharma | first=Deepanshu | title=Who is Richard Robson? Australian Chemist Who Won The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025 | website=The Daily Guardian | date=8 October 2025 | url=https://thedailyguardian.com/world/australia/who-is-richard-robson-australian-chemist-who-won-the-nobel-prize-in-chemistry-2025-669544/ | access-date=8 October 2025}}</ref> He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Outstanding Academy Fellows elected to Royal Society |url=https://www.science.org.au/news-and-events/news-and-media-releases/outstanding-academy-fellows-elected-royal-society |access-date=10 May 2022 |website=Australian Academy of Science |language=en}}</ref>

Robson shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his early contribution to the field of [[metal–organic framework]]s (MOFs).

== Personal life ==
His daughter is former TV presenter [[Naomi Robson]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fiona |first1=Byrne |title='Still pinching myself': Naomi Robson 'so proud' of her Nobel Prize-winning dad |url=https://www.heraldsun.com.au/entertainment/confidential/still-pinching-myself-naomi-robson-so-proud-of-her-nobel-prizewinning-dad/news-story/b97ab8a4b9361f90519aa394cdb703d0 |work=[[Herald Sun]] |date=2025-12-13}}</ref>
